newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Visit to Nigeria by U.N. rights officers delayed.
newsitem.headline: Visit to Nigeria by U.N. rights officers delayed.

text.p: Two human rights special rapporteurs due to arrive Nigeria on Sunday to investigate alleged rights abuses have delayed their visit until after "certain clarifications" have been made with the military government, their aide said.

Bacre Waly Ndiaye, a Senegalese who is the U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, and Param Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian U.N. special rapporteur on independence of judges and lawyers, were to stay until March 5.
"The U.N. human rights special rapporteurs will definitely not be arriving today," Alan Parra, an officer at the U.N. Centre for Human Rights in Geneva, told Reuters in Lagos.
"We are seeking certain clarifications on the visit from the Nigerian government. I cannot go into further details," said Parra, in Nigeria since Wednesday preparing for the visit.

But Auwalu Yadudu, special adviser to the Nigerian government on legal matters, told Reuters by telephone from the capital Abuja that he was unaware of the delay, adding: "We have made ready all arrangements for the visit of the U.N. team."
A senior state official said earlier: "We are taking the visit seriously because human rights is now an important issue worldwide."
The team was due to visit several big cities including Abuja, Lagos, Kaduna, Kano and Port Harcourt.

The U.N. human rights commission called for the two-man visit after another mission visiting Nigeria last year called for the support of the government's democracy programme but said it found human rights "terrible".

The government of General Sani Abacha turned a pariah in 1995 after it hanged nine minority rights activists, including author Ken Saro-Wiwa for murder after a trial judged unfair by international experts. Another 19 Ogoni youths facing similar charges are now in detention.

Many people, including former military ruler Olusegun Obasanjo, his deputy Shehu Musa Yar'Adua and four journalists are behind bars for allegedly plotting to overthrow Abacha, who seized power five months after a previous army ruler annulled a June 1993 poll to restore democracy.
Moshood Abiola, presumed winner of the poll has been held since June 1994 for proclaiming himself president. Dozens of those in opposition to the government are also in detention.
Africa's most populous country of 100 million people has been in crisis since the poll was annulled.
Western diplomats said the success of the visit by the U.N. team would be measured by whether they were allowed to meet high-profile detainees like Abiola.
"The rapporteurs will not meet convicted prisoners. If they request to see other detainees this will be considered strictly in accordance with the terms of their visit," said an official.
Abacha's government has been vocal in criticising what it called foreign interference in Nigeria's domestic affairs.
Despite local and foreign criticisms it is implementing its own transition to democracy with October 1, 1998 as the target date to hand over to a democratically-elected president.
One senior government official said: "Once there is military rule you can't expect human rights to be perfect."

The investigators will report back to the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission. Nigeria will be one of the countries in the dock when the main U.N. human rights forum opens its annual six-week meeting in Geneva on March 10.
